title: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions
transcript: The mean shares a total equally among the readings. If a mean and its count are known, multiply to restore the total. When combining groups, put the totals together and divide by the total number of readings.

AMC practice questions can describe average scores, measurements or totals over several days. Write the number of readings beside each mean. A Rossmoyne style average puzzle can give overlapping groups. Restoring their totals exposes a shared reading.
Find the mean of three readings: ten, sixteen and nineteen. State what a mean represents for these readings. Imagine redistributing the total to three equal amounts.
The three readings sum to forty-five. Keep all three values when finding the total. Divide by three. Each equal share is fifteen, so that is the mean.
One group has three values with mean thirty-one. A second group has seven values with mean eleven. Find the mean after combining the two groups. They contain different numbers of readings.

The first total is ninety-three. The second is seventy-seven. Compute each by multiplying its mean by its count. The combined total is one hundred and seventy from ten readings. Divide this total by the combined count. The combined mean is seventeen. It lies between the two means and closer to the larger group's mean.
There are seven readings with mean one hundred and two over seven. The first four have mean twenty-nine over two. The last four have mean fifteen. Exactly one reading is in both groups. Find it.

Recover the first and last totals by multiplying the means by their counts. The first total is fifty-eight and the last is sixty. The total of the full list is one hundred and two. Adding the first and last totals counts the shared reading twice. The excess above the whole list is sixteen. This is the one shared reading.

There are exactly as many distinct positions as the first count plus the last count minus one. That explains why the total correction is a single value. Add the totals and remove one copy of sixteen. You recover one hundred and two, the total for the stated overall mean.

A group with more readings has more weight. Add the original totals instead of sharing the two means equally. A reading shared by two groups contributes to both totals. Count one fewer copy in the full collection.
Write mean, count and total together. Start each calculation with the pair you actually know. Check the groups for overlap and the final denominator for how many readings there really are.
